exp-conjugates-and-rationalising#1.en:
Answer the WHOLE of this question without a calculator.
Simplify:  ∛54 − ∛16

exp-conjugates-and-rationalising#2.en: Prime factors first, as always — but count carefully. Under a cube root a factor needs three of itself before it earns a ticket out, not two.

exp-conjugates-and-rationalising#3.en: Rewrite every base as a product of prime factors first, then look for the factors with tickets out — under a cube root that means groups of three.

exp-conjugates-and-rationalising#7.en: REMEMBER: the root index is what decides how many of a factor you need. A square root wants pairs; a cube root wants threes. 2⁴ = 2³ · 2 hands ONE 2 out of a cube root and leaves one behind — it does not hand out two.

exp-conjugates-and-rationalising#8.en: Two cube roots that look nothing alike turn out to be helpings of the same thing, and prime factors are what show it. Under ∛54 sits 2 · 3³: the three 3s travel together and walk out as a single 3, leaving the lonely 2 behind. Under ∛16 sits 2⁴, which is one complete group of three 2s plus a spare, so a 2 walks out and a 2 stays. Both land on ∛2, and once the roots are identical, subtracting them is counting: three of them take away two of them leaves one of them. Write that 1 in front before you tidy it away — it is the line that shows the marker you were counting, not guessing.

exp-conjugates-and-rationalising#10.en: Do not multiply this out term by term — look at the two brackets and notice how they differ. And be careful about what the 2 out front does when you square it.

exp-conjugates-and-rationalising#11.en: Same two terms, only the middle sign differs — that is a diff in □'s, so it collapses straight to first squared minus second squared:

exp-conjugates-and-rationalising#14.en: WATCH OUT: (2√3)² is 2² × (√3)² = 4 × 3 = 12, not 2 × 3 = 6. Everything inside the bracket gets squared, the coefficient included.

exp-conjugates-and-rationalising#15.en: This is the reason conjugates work at all, met on its own before you need it in a fraction. When two brackets hold the same two terms and differ only in the middle sign, the cross terms cancel each other out exactly, and all that survives is the square of the first minus the square of the second. Squaring is what kills the surds — √3 squared is just 3 — so a product that looked full of roots lands on a plain whole number. Hold on to that: it is precisely the move that clears a surd out of a denominator in part (d).

exp-conjugates-and-rationalising#17.en: A bracket squared is that bracket times itself — so it keeps a middle term. Write it out in three pieces before you simplify anything.

exp-conjugates-and-rationalising#18.en: Squaring a binomial keeps the middle term — first squared, plus twice first times second, plus second squared:

exp-conjugates-and-rationalising#22.en: REMEMBER: (√7 + √2)² ≠ 7 + 2. That is the BIG NO-NO wearing a different hat — a square never distributes over a + or a −, and the middle term is exactly what it leaves behind when you try.

exp-conjugates-and-rationalising#23.en: Put this part next to (b) and the pair teaches the whole story. Same-signs-differ gave you a clean whole number, because the two cross terms cancelled. Same-signs-match keeps both cross terms, and 2 lots of √7 × √2 is 2√14 — which cannot be tidied any further, because 14 has no square factors to hand out tickets to. So the answer stays in two pieces, a whole-number part and a surd part, and that is a perfectly finished answer. Notice how √7 × √2 became √14: multiplying two square roots means multiplying what is underneath them, which is one of the surd laws that is genuinely allowed. Adding them is the one that is not.

exp-conjugates-and-rationalising#25.en: Start on the left and drive it down to what you were given. The denominator has two terms, so it has a conjugate — and watch what the denominator turns into once you use it.

exp-conjugates-and-rationalising#26.en: A “show that” is worked from one side only — start on the left. The denominator is a two-term surd, so multiply by the conjugate over itself:

exp-conjugates-and-rationalising#31.en: WATCH OUT: x ≠ 4 is not decoration. At x = 4 the denominator √x − 2 is 0 and the whole expression is undefined — division by zero, which is a different word from “no solution”. That is why the question hands you the restriction, and why you may cancel the (x − 4) safely everywhere else.

exp-conjugates-and-rationalising#32.en: The conjugate trick is not only for numbers. Here the denominator is √x − 2, so its conjugate is √x + 2, and multiplying by that over itself is multiplying by 1 — the expression's value never changes, only its shape. What makes this one satisfying is what the denominator becomes: (√x)² − 2² is x − 4, which is already sitting in the numerator, so the whole thing cancels and the fraction disappears. That is the pattern to recognise, because the difference of two squares turns up constantly in this disguise — x − 4 IS (√x)² − 2² whenever x is positive. And the restriction matters for exactly the reason the cancelling works: you are dividing top and bottom by x − 4, which is only legal while x − 4 is not zero.

exp-first-step-and-method#1.en:
Answer the WHOLE of this question without a calculator.
Simplify:  √48 + √300 − √27

exp-first-step-and-method#2.en: Break every number under the root into its prime factors first. Then hunt for factors that come in pairs — those are the ones with tickets out.

exp-first-step-and-method#3.en: Rewrite every base as a product of prime factors first — that is the only way to see which factors have tickets out.

exp-first-step-and-method#5.en: A factor may leave the root when its exponent matches the root index — here, in pairs.

exp-first-step-and-method#8.en: REMEMBER: √x + √y ≠ √(x + y). You may only add or subtract surds once every one of them is the same √ — and then it is nothing more than 4x + 10x − 3x = 11x.

exp-first-step-and-method#9.en: Three surds that look completely unrelated turn out to be three helpings of the same thing, and prime factors are what show you that. Under √48 there is a 2⁴, which is two pairs of 2s, so a 4 walks out and a 3 stays behind. Under √300 there is a 2² and a 5², so a 2 and a 5 walk out as 10, and again a 3 stays behind. Under √27 there is 3³, which is one pair of 3s and a spare, so a 3 walks out and a 3 stays. Every single one lands on √3 — and once they are the same √, adding them is just counting: 4 of them plus 10 of them minus 3 of them. A factor only earns its ticket out when its exponent matches the root index, which for a square root means pairs; that is the whole rule, and it is why you factorise before you do anything else.

exp-first-step-and-method#11.en: Start on the left-hand side and drive it down to what you were given. Multiply top and bottom by the conjugate of the denominator — the same two surds with the middle sign swapped.

exp-first-step-and-method#12.en: Work on the left-hand side only and drive it down to what is given.

exp-first-step-and-method#14.en: Multiplying by the conjugate over itself is multiplying by 1, so nothing changes — but the denominator turns into a difference of squares and the surd disappears.

exp-first-step-and-method#17.en: WATCH OUT: the conjugate changes only the sign in the middle — the conjugate of √5 − √2 is √5 + √2, not −√5 + √2. And do not start from the right-hand side: a “show that” is worked from one side only.

exp-first-step-and-method#18.en: A “show that” is a one-way trip. You are handed the destination, so the marks are for the journey — start on the side you were given and keep going until it turns into the other side. Never start from the answer and work backwards; that proves nothing, because you would be assuming the very thing you were asked to show. The engine here is the conjugate: (√5 − √2)(√5 + √2) is a difference of squares, so it collapses to 5 − 2 = 3, a plain number with no root left in it. And because you multiplied the top by the same thing you multiplied the bottom by, you multiplied the whole fraction by 1 — its value never moved, only its appearance.

exp-first-step-and-method#20.en: There is a + between the terms, so nothing may cancel yet. Divorce every power into 3ˣ times a small number first, then look for the common factor.

exp-first-step-and-method#21.en: There is a + between the terms, so every power gets divorced first: 3x+1 = 3ˣ · 3  and  3x−1 = 3ˣ · 3⁻¹.

exp-first-step-and-method#23.en: Now take out the common factor — always the base carrying the variable exponent.

exp-first-step-and-method#24.en: = 3ˣ(3 + 1/3) / 3ˣ(1 + 1/9)   — the + signs are now caged, so 3ˣ may cancel

exp-first-step-and-method#26.en: Dividing by a fraction is KFC — keep, flip, change.

exp-first-step-and-method#28.en: WATCH OUT: never cancel 3ˣ across a + or a − before it is caged inside a bracket. That one move is exactly what the “caged” rule exists to stop.

exp-first-step-and-method#29.en: The + sign is the whole difficulty here. Cancelling is division, and you may only divide a whole top by a whole bottom — so while the top is a sum of two separate things, 3ˣ is not a factor of it and may not be crossed out. Divorcing is what fixes that: 3<sup>x+1</sup> is nothing more mysterious than 3ˣ multiplied by 3, and 3<sup>x−1</sup> is 3ˣ multiplied by 1/3. Once every term has a visible 3ˣ in it, you can bracket the rest out and the 3ˣ becomes a genuine factor of the whole top and the whole bottom — caged — and only then is it allowed to cancel. What is left is two ordinary fractions divided by each other, and the x has vanished completely: the answer is the plain number 3, whatever x happens to be.

exp-first-step-and-method#30.en:
No calculator.
Given that 2x = a and 3x = b, write 72x in terms of a and b.

exp-first-step-and-method#31.en: Prime factors first — always. Split 72 into powers of 2 and 3, and then read the power-of-a-power law backwards.

exp-first-step-and-method#35.en: REMEMBER: 23x = (2x)³ — power of a power works in both directions, and reading it backwards is what turns the question into a and b.

exp-first-step-and-method#36.en: You are given 2<sup>x</sup> and 3<sup>x</sup>, so the only useful shape for 72<sup>x</sup> is one built out of 2<sup>x</sup> and 3<sup>x</sup> — which means 72 has to be pulled apart into 2s and 3s before anything else happens. That gives 2³ · 3², and raising a product to the power x hands the x to both factors: 2<sup>3x</sup> · 3<sup>2x</sup>. The last move is the one people miss. You already know the law (2<sup>x</sup>)³ = 2<sup>3x</sup> going left to right; here you need it going right to left, regrouping 2<sup>3x</sup> as (2<sup>x</sup>)³ so that the a you were handed can be slotted straight in. Same law, read the other way round.
